intro: One oak in downtown Athens is said to own itself, along with the land within eight feet of its trunk. The tree standing on the corner of South Finley and Dearing today is the successor, raised from an acorn of the original and planted in 1946 after a windstorm took its parent. As far as Athens is concerned, the deed came with the acorn. There is a historical marker, a street corner, no fence and no fee, and a question of property law that nobody has ever bothered to settle in court.
meta_description: An oak in downtown Athens is said to own itself. The Son of the Tree That Owns Itself was planted in 1946 from its parent's acorn.
question_meta: The Son of the Tree That Owns Itself stands at South Finley and Dearing in Athens, Georgia, planted in 1946 from the original's acorn.
question_answer: The tree Athens is known for is the Son of the Tree That Owns Itself, a white oak of about eighty years standing on the corner of South Finley Street and Dearing Street, downtown. It is not the oldest tree in the city and it is the one worth the walk: it was planted on 4 December 1946, grown from an acorn of the original oak that fell in a windstorm in 1942. That original was, by a story the Athens Weekly Banner published in 1890, deeded ownership of itself and of the ground within eight feet of its trunk by Colonel William H. Jackson. Legal scholars doubt that a tree can hold property. Athens has never let the objection interfere. The plot is public, free and open at every hour, with a historical marker on the corner.
question_context: The corner of South Finley Street and Dearing Street sits on the western edge of downtown Athens, a few minutes on foot from the University of Georgia's North Campus and from Broad Street. There is nothing to book and no visitor centre. The plot is a corner of ground with a marker and a set of steps, and the tree on it is a white oak of ordinary size, because it is only eighty years old. The gap between the size of the tree and the size of the story is the visit. The original oak stood here for as long as anyone in Athens could remember and came down in a windstorm in 1942. The Junior Ladies Garden Club had thought ahead: they had an acorn from it, grew the seedling on, and planted it in the same plot on 4 December 1946, with horticulture students from the university doing the digging. Street parking is the usual approach. Nothing here is gated, ticketed or closed at night, which under the terms of the legend is only proper.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Athens, Georgia?
faq.a: The tree Athens is known for is not its oldest. The Son of the Tree That Owns Itself is a white oak of about eighty years, planted in 1946 from an acorn of the original that stood on the same corner and fell in 1942.

faq.q: Does the tree really own itself?
faq.a: By local tradition, yes. A story published in 1890 says Colonel William H. Jackson deeded the original tree ownership of itself and of the land within eight feet of its trunk. Legal scholars regard that as impossible under property law, and nobody has taken it to court to find out.

faq.q: Is it free to visit, and when is it open?
faq.a: Free, and open at any hour. It stands on a public street corner with a historical marker, no fence and no gate.

It is on the corner of South Finley Street and Dearing Street, on the western edge of downtown Athens, a short walk from Broad Street and the University of Georgia's North Campus. Street parking nearby.

trees.story: This oak is the son of a tree that, by local legend, owned itself. The Athens Weekly Banner ran the story in 1890: Colonel William H. Jackson, fond of the white oak he had played under as a boy, deeded the tree ownership of itself and of the land within eight feet of its trunk. Legal scholars have picked holes in it ever since, on the reasonable ground that a tree cannot hold property, and Athens has never much minded. The original came down in a windstorm in 1942. On 4 December 1946 the Junior Ladies Garden Club planted a seedling raised from one of its acorns in the same plot, five feet tall and trimmed back to three for the move, with University of Georgia horticulture students turning the soil. It passed fifty feet by 2006. So the tree on the corner of South Finley and Dearing is about eighty years old rather than two hundred, and what it inherited was an acorn and a deed. Read it that way and it gets better rather than worse: the legend belongs to a tree that fell, and this one carries the name and the plot. A historical marker stands at the corner. There is no gate, no fee and no opening hours, and by the terms of a will nobody has ever tested in court, no landlord either.
